QF.id: AIFM CII Fund Performance and Benchmarking_23

question.text: Why are Sharpe ratio and Sortino ratio less directly applicable as headline performance metrics for Category I/II AIFs than for listed-equity portfolios?

answer.text: Sharpe and Sortino are SEBI-prohibited for Cat I/II AIFs.
Cat I/II AIFs invest in illiquid, unlisted securities without regular observable price series, making volatility (standard deviation) hard to compute meaningfully — IRR/TVPI/DPI are more apt.
Sharpe and Sortino require a negative risk-free rate.
Cat I/II AIFs always have zero beta, so the ratios are undefined.

explanation.text: The Logic: Sharpe = (Rp - Rf)/σp and Sortino uses downside deviation. Both require a time series of returns and a defensible volatility estimate. Cat I/II AIF portfolios are dominated by illiquid, unlisted holdings without regular observable prices; valuations are typically quarterly mark-to-model. The resulting standard-deviation estimate is smoothed and stale, so Sharpe/Sortino computed from it can be artificially flattering. Cash-flow-based metrics (IRR, MOIC, TVPI, DPI, RVPI, PME, Direct Alpha) are therefore preferred as headline performance measures for Cat I/II AIFs. The Trap: SEBI does not prohibit Sharpe/Sortino (A). The risk-free rate is positive (C). Cat I/II beta is unobservable, not literally zero (D). Note: The XIX-D workbook discusses Cat I/II illiquidity, J-curve behaviour, IRR, DPI, RVPI, TVPI, MOIC, PME, Direct Alpha, and benchmarking agencies, but does not specifically describe Sharpe/Sortino or downside deviation or the volatility/illiquidity-smoothing trade-off above. Treat that framing as general performance-measurement knowledge applicable when interpreting Cat I/II reports.
